newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Proliferating currencies divide embattled Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Proliferating currencies divide embattled Zaire.

text.p: Monetary madness is dividing embattled Zaire as Tutsi-led rebels advance from the east.
Economists say the sprawling nation now has six rival modes of exchange or currency zones.

"You have a different exchange rate for the normal new zaire, the 'prostate' new zaire, the old zaire note still in circulation in Kasai, a separate rate in Shaba, separate rates on bank cheques," one Western economist told Reuters.
Then there is the U.S. dollar "which circulates as an alternative national currency".
New larger denomination zaire bills issued by the central bank in January are nicknamed "prostates", an irreverent reference to President Mobutu Sese Seko's prostate cancer.
The appearance of "prostates" on Kinshasa's chaotic money market triggered instant hyper-inflation with the prices of some basic commodities doubling overnight.
But an effective popular boycott of the new notes stabilised the inflation rate in the capital at below five percent in February, according to the European Union.
With major international oil companies joining the boycott last Friday, the government looked set to abandon the notes.

"There has not been an official decision either from the bank or the government as yet. But I think that the blockage is such that the bills will have to be brought back into the bank," Pascale Dema, the prime minister's spokesman, told Reuters.

In a desperate bid to get hold of hard currency to pay for the war in the east, the government had been paying up to four times the normal rate of the new zaire exchanging "prostates" for dollars, a commercial banker in the capital told Reuters.
Officially the government printed the new one million, half a million and 100,000 notes to make up for a shortfall in local currency supplies at the central bank.
The cost of printing smaller denomination notes already in circulation had become much higher than the value of the smallest 5,000 and 1,000 new zaires.
The government had too few smaller notes even in 50,000 denominations to pay the unwieldy civil service and army but even civil servants refused to accept the new larger bills.
Enterprising money changers, operating like a mafia clique, are making up to 100 percent profits on exchange rates between the country's different provinces.
Differences in rates between Kinshasa and diamond rich Kasai, which retained old one million zaire notes superseded in 1992, offer opportunities to the enterprising money changer.
One Zairean economist said Kasaians had printed "real fake" zaires in Argentina and Brazil to replace disintegrating notes and keep their rival currency going.
On the streets of Kinshasa, the "prostate" exchanges for almost twice the rate to the U.S. dollar as older and smaller denomination notes, money changers say.

Kinshasa boycotted the new bills but Lubumbashi, provincial capital of the copper-rich province of Shaba, was flooded with them. The exchange rate there last week reached almost four times the rate in Kinshasa at 450,000 new zaires to the dollar.

"The professional money changers are making up to 100 percent profits transporting prostates between Kinshasa and Lubumbashi and exchanging them against the dollar," says Pascale, 29, a university graduate who makes his money on Kinshasa's "Wall Street" black market.
